@cybergibbons @wesmorgan1 Appliances that can't run on a lighting circuit have special 110V plugs. You have to realize that there were only lighting circuits in homes until about 1960. Got a toaster? You screwed in a lightbulb socket with a 110V outlet on it. Old homes are often a hybrid still.

https://x.com/cybergibbons/status/1221578437095120897

1221747369571749888.a: @cybergibbons @wesmorgan1 This was the only way to plugin anything in my father's 19th century home and these are still commonly used. you got one with a pull chain so you can run your appliance with the lights off. Often you just taped the wall switch on. t.co

1221748052417024000.a: @cybergibbons @wesmorgan1 These were in the ceiling of course so you often had extension cords stapled across the ceiling and down the wall... Obviously this is why other countries developed better standards... This was a constant source of house fire obviously.

1221757352183058433.a: @cybergibbons @wesmorgan1 This is a 110V appliance outlet. Lamps have two vertical prongs, appliances have one or two horizontal + optional ground. Our 1950s home had 2 appliance outlets in the kitchen and ceiling lamps. Other rooms had a switched outlet for lamps and one unswitched for a clock or radio. t.co
